answers: Master data covers: chart of accounts, companies (us, customers, suppliers), catalogue service items, and VAT rates — each as its own object; companies also store an IBAN where known.

So when we talk about master data, we've got a few different things going on — there's the chart of accounts, then all the companies we work with (that's ourselves, our customers, and our suppliers), plus the services we offer listed as catalogue items, and on top of that the VAT rates, and every single one of those becomes its own master-data object; oh, and each company record also holds that company's bank account number, the IBAN, whenever we actually have it.

The master data splits into its own object for each of these: the chart of accounts, the companies we deal with (our own outfit, customers, suppliers), the services we flog as catalogue items, and the VAT rates; any company we've got a bank number for also carries that IBAN on its record.

Sales invoices we issue are recorded as sales_invoice documents with these fields: number, issue date, seller and buyer (looked up by NIP), net amount, currency, and VAT rate code. VAT = net × rate% ÷ 100, rounded half up to the grosz; gross = net + VAT; due date = issue date + payment days from the invoice; status begins as open, moves to paid when matched. Open amount starts at gross and decreases as payments are matched; partly paid invoices remain open; reversing a match reopens a paid invoice. Booking is in pl-stat: debit 201 for gross, credit 701 for net, credit 222 for VAT.

So whenever we send out a sales invoice, it gets entered into the system as a document of type sales_invoice, and it carries all of the following: the invoice number, the issue date, the seller and the buyer — both looked up using their NIP — the net amount, the currency, and the VAT rate code straight from the invoice. Now, to calculate VAT, you take the net amount, multiply it by the rate's percentage, divide by 100, and then round that result half up to the nearest grosz. The gross is simply net plus VAT. The due date is calculated by adding the number of payment days printed on the invoice to the issue date. The status field starts out as open and can eventually move to paid once payments are matched against it. The open amount begins equal to the gross and gets reduced as payments come in and are matched; if it's only partly paid, the invoice stays open, and if a match gets undone on a fully paid invoice, it flips back to open again. For the accounting side, every one of these invoices gets posted in the pl-stat book: account 201 gets debited for the gross, account 701 gets credited for the net, and account 222 gets credited for the VAT.

Each invoice we send out lands in the system as a sales_invoice — it grabs the number, issue date, seller and buyer by NIP, net amount, currency, and VAT rate code off the invoice. VAT is net times the rate percent over 100, half-up rounded to the grosz; gross is net plus that VAT; due date is issue date plus however many payment days the invoice shows. Status kicks off as open, flips to paid when matched. Open amount starts at gross and drops as payments get matched in — partly paid stays open, and if you undo a match on a paid one it goes back to open. It all gets booked in pl-stat: 201 debited for the gross, 701 credited for the net, 222 credited for the VAT.

A supplier's invoice turns into a purchase_invoice document with these fields: number, invoice date, supplier looked up by NIP, our company as owner, net amount, currency, and VAT rate code. VAT equals net multiplied by the rate's percent divided by 100, rounded half up to the grosz; gross is net plus VAT. Status begins as open and moves to paid once matched; open amount starts at gross and decreases as payments are matched. A partly matched invoice stays open; undoing a match on a paid invoice puts it back to open. Every purchase invoice posts in book pl-stat: debit 402 for the net, debit 221 for the VAT, credit 202 for the gross.

So when a supplier sends us an invoice, what we do is create a document of type purchase_invoice, and we fill in the number, the invoice date, we look up the supplier using their NIP, we set our own company as the owner, and we record the net amount, the currency, and the VAT rate code. Now, the VAT amount — that's calculated by taking the net, multiplying it by the rate's percent, dividing by 100, and then rounding half up to the grosz, and once we've got that, the gross is simply net plus VAT. The status on that document kicks off as open, and it moves to paid as payments get matched against it; the open amount starts at the full gross and ticks down with each matched payment. If it's only partly matched, it stays open; and if someone undoes a match on a paid invoice, it flips back to open again. In the books — that's book pl-stat — every one of these purchase invoices gets posted with a debit on 402 for the net, a debit on 221 for the VAT, and a credit on 202 for the gross.

Basically, a supplier invoice comes in and we slap it into the system as a purchase_invoice — fields are: number, invoice date, supplier pulled up by NIP, our company as owner, net amount, currency, VAT rate code. VAT's worked out as net times the rate percent over 100, half-up rounded to the grosz, and gross is just net plus that VAT. It starts life with status open, flips to paid as payments get matched, with the open amount kicking off at gross and dropping as matches come in. Partly paid? Still open. Undo a match on a paid one? Back to open. Book pl-stat gets the entry: 402 debited for the net, 221 debited for the VAT, 202 credited for the gross.

Each bank statement line is stored as a bank_line record with date, amount, currency, direction, title (used as reference), counterparty and counterparty account, and our account; open amount is initialized to the amount, and status begins as open, flipping to settled once open amount hits zero. Incoming money is matched to open sales invoices for the customer identified by the sending account, tried in sequence: exact title match; title match with up to 0.02 shortfall or excess, difference written off to 755; single invoice of identical amount; fewest invoices summing to the amount, maximum 4; partial match to the named invoice; otherwise oldest open invoices consumed in order until funds run out. Outgoing money follows the same sequence against open purchase invoices for the supplier identified by the receiving account, but without the 0.02 tolerance. Each match reduces the open amounts on both the invoices and the bank line by the allocated figure, marking each as paid or settled when nothing remains open, and records one settlement entry per invoice capturing the payment, document type and id, amount, and date. A tolerated difference produces a matching difference record holding kind, amount, currency, direction, account, and date, and a shortfall difference is posted in book pl-stat as a debit to the difference account and a credit to 201. Anything left unmatched is displayed as a side-by-side view of open bank lines and open invoices for manual pairing.

So basically what happens is: every single line on a bank statement gets turned into a bank_line record — you've got your date on there, the amount, the currency, which direction the money's going, the title becomes the reference, then the counterparty plus their account, and our account too; the open amount kicks off equal to the full amount, and the status starts out as open and only switches over to settled once there's nothing left open. Now for money coming in, the system goes hunting through the open sales invoices belonging to whichever customer's account the money came from, and it tries a bunch of things in order: first it looks for the invoice that matches the title exactly; then it'll still accept that invoice if the amount is off by up to 0.02 either way, writing the difference off to account 755; next it looks for any single invoice that's exactly that amount; then it tries to find the smallest combination of invoices that adds up to it, but it won't use more than 4; after that it'll partially pay the named invoice; and if none of that works, it just chews through the oldest open invoices until the money runs out. Money going out works exactly the same way but it's matched against open purchase invoices for the supplier whose account is receiving it, and there's no tolerance on that side. Whenever a match happens, the open amounts on the invoices and on the bank line both get reduced by whatever was allocated — things get marked paid or settled once they're fully cleared — and the system writes a settlement record for each invoice that got touched, with the payment, document type and id, amount, and date all in there. If a tolerated difference came into play, that gets its own matching difference record with kind, amount, currency, direction, account, and date, and specifically when it's a shortfall, there's a posting in the pl-stat book: debit goes to the difference account, credit goes to 201. Anything the whole process couldn't sort out just sits in a side-by-side view — open lines on one side, open invoices on the other — waiting for a person to manually match them up.

Bank statement lines become bank_line records — date, amount, currency, direction, title as reference, counterparty and counterparty account, our account; open amount equals amount at the start, status is open, goes settled when open amount clears. Inbound cash hits open sales invoices of the customer whose account sent it: title-named invoice first; that invoice if amount is off by at most 0.02, difference to 755; one invoice for the exact amount; fewest invoices totaling it, cap of 4; named invoice partially; oldest open invoices in order until exhausted. Outbound cash runs the same logic against open purchase invoices of the destination supplier's account, no tolerance. A match cuts open amounts on invoices and line by the allocated figure, marks each paid or settled when zeroed, logs one settlement per invoice: payment, document type and id, amount, date. A tolerated difference writes a matching difference record: kind, amount, currency, direction, account, date; a shortfall posts in pl-stat, debit to the difference account, credit to 201. Unresolved lines and invoices sit open side by side for manual matching.

Complaints get logged as complaint docs with a number, customer, and details — each one auto-opens a case-type record where the subject is that complaint number and status begins at open, then can shift to resolved.

So here's how it works: when a complaint comes in, you create a complaint document that holds the number, the customer, and the details. That complaint document then kicks off a brand-new follow-up record — its type is literally called case, the subject field gets set to the complaint number, and the status field starts out as open, though it can be changed to resolved down the line.

Every complaint gets its own complaint doc — number, customer, details — and that kicks off a follow-up case where subject equals the complaint number and status kicks off as open, moving to resolved when done.
A withdrawn complaint gets its case marked resolved.
So basically, if a customer decides to pull back their complaint, what happens is that the case associated with it ends up being resolved — that's just how it works.
Customer pulls the complaint, the case closes out as resolved.
